stories.title: NBA Referees Association weighs in on LaMelo Ball's traveling no-call
stories.summary: The National Basketball Referees Association (NBRA) responded to the controversial traveling no-call by Minnesota Timberwolves guard LaMelo Ball.
stories.detailText: The National Basketball Referees Association (NBRA), the official union of NBA officials, responded to the controversial traveling no-call by Minnesota Timberwolves guard LaMelo Ball , indicating that it should have been ruled as an infraction. “For everyone asking, ‘how is this legal?’ It’s not!” the NBRA posted Thursday, Oct. 22 from its social media account. “He gathers with his right foot on the floor and would be permitted two steps by rule (left-right). He takes four steps after gathering the ball and travels.” The play occurred with 8:19 left in the second quarter of Minnesota’s game against the Miami Heat . With the game tied at 39, Ball slipped past a screen toward the right side of the floor. Ball picked up his dribble and then took a gather step by shuffling to his right. The issue is that Ball then took four lateral steps before beginning his shooting motion. He would go on to lace the 3-pointer, one of his five successful conversions on the night. For everyone asking, “how is this legal?” It’s not! He gathers with his right foot on the floor and would be permitted two steps by rule (left-right). He takes four steps after gathering the ball and travels. https://t.co/dSitGeRNSD — NBA Referees (@OfficialNBARefs) October 22, 2026 The Timberwolves won the game, 131-106, spoiling the Heat debut of Giannis Antetokounmpo . When reached for comment on the no-call, the NBA referred USA TODAY Sports to the statement issued by the NBRA. This was the latest controversial traveling no-call early in the 2026-27 season. On opening night Tuesday, Oct. 20, Oklahoma City Thunder guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander shuffled his pivot foot on a converted field goal, drawing a number of critical comments from fans and viewers on social media. During the preseason, Boston Celtics guard Hugo González was on his way to an uncontested layup on a fast break when he collected the ball at the 3-point line and then took five steps before laying it in. That play was also not called for a travel. The NBA and its officiating staff review every play during the season and assess the enforcement of its rules, so they may opt to take a closer look should they deem it a larger issue. At this point, however, the gather step and travels have not risen to that level. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: NBA Referees Association weighs in on LaMelo Ball's traveling no-call

stories.title: President Trump criticizes 76ers' LeBron James for actions amid national anthem
stories.summary: President Donald Trump has accused LeBron James of disrespecting the U.S. after the 76ers star appeared to continue his warmups during the national anthem.
stories.detailText: President Donald Trump on Thursday accused LeBron James of disrespecting the United States after the 76ers star appeared to continue his warmups while the national anthem was performed before Philadelphia's season opener Tuesday against the Knicks in New York. James appeared to practice a golf swing and jump shot during "The Star-Spangled Banner" at Madison Square Garden. James, in his debut for the 76ers, was lined up alongside teammates who mostly stood still during the anthem. "I said right from the beginning that he's no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE," Trump said of James in a social media post sharing the video. "LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!" Representatives for James did not respond to requests for comment from ESPN. James, 41, in his record-24th NBA season, was set to make his home debut for the Sixers on Thursday night against Cleveland . Trump himself also has been criticized for his actions during the national anthem. In 2020, the Miami Herald posted a video of Trump waving his hands as if to conduct an orchestra while the national anthem was played at a Super Bowl watch party. In the brief video clip, Trump also appeared to gesture at others as those around him stood with hand over heart while the anthem was played. Trump and James have been critical of each other for years, occasionally trading public swipes. Among some of the more notable times James became entangled with the president or politics: • James was with the Cavaliers in 2017 when he made a statement during an NBA game with his shoes -- one black, one white, with the word "equality" in capital gold letters on the back of each. Then, after the game, James made a statement about Trump, saying: "This is a beautiful country and we're never going to let one person dictate how beautiful and how powerful we are." James had called Trump "a bum" on Twitter and also said earlier that season of the president: "He doesn't understand how many kids, no matter the race, look up to the president of the United States for guidance, for leadership, for words of encouragement. He doesn't understand that, and that's what makes me more sick than anything." • James spoke out on social issues and the nation's political climate after Fox News host Laura Ingraham criticized the then-three-time NBA champion for his 2018 comments about social issues. "We will definitely not shut up and dribble," he said. "I will definitely not do that. I mean too much to society. I mean too much to the youth. I mean too much to so many kids that feel like they don't have a way out and they need someone to help lead them out of the situation they're in." James referenced Muhammad Ali, Jim Brown, Bill Russell and Jackie Robinson as athletes who previously spoke up for equality and change with no concerns about the consequences or any rewards. "We know it's bigger than us," James said. James was named The Associated Press Male Athlete of the Year in 2020 in large part for leading the Los Angeles Lakers to a championship and helped convince many people -- at the peak of Black Lives Matter -- who had never voted to finally head to the polls. "I still know what I do on the floor and obviously, I give everything to the game," James said. "But I can make a greater impact off the floor right now, more than I can on the floor. And I want to continue to inspire people with the way I play the game of basketball. But there's so many more things that I can do off the floor to help cultivate people, inspire people, bring people together, empower them." Information from ESPN's Dave McMenamin and The Associated Press was used in this report.

stories.title: Paul George draws NBA season's first fine for flopping after league reviews Celtics-Pistons game
stories.summary: During the offseason, the NBA said it would emphasize 'secondary, theatrical and exaggerated movement' with flopping fines for the 2026-27 season.
stories.detailText: Paul George had a historic debut with the Boston Celtics on Tuesday that later earned another notable footnote. George, 36, tallied 38 points in Boston's 121-113 loss to the Detroit Pistons, setting a franchise record for most points scored in a Celtics debut. Additionally, he shot 7-of-12 on 3-pointers, passing Kyle Korver for eighth on the NBA's all-time 3-point shots made list. Following the game, George drew the season's first fine for flopping on a fourth-quarter collision at midcourt with Detroit's Duncan Robinson. No call was made during the game, but the league issued a $2,000 fine after reviewing the play. The league fined Paul George $2,000 for flopping after reviewing a play from Boston's opening-night loss. More fines please! The NBA is healing 🙏 pic.twitter.com/j03J5R6Sc5 — Jacob (@Jacobtheclipper) October 22, 2026 The postgame penalty was part of the NBA's emphasis this season to crack down on "STEM" violations — or Secondary, Theatrical, Exaggerated Movements attempting to draw foul calls. "It's just something that we've seen that doesn't present well in-game, live or on TV, and it's not the fabric of NBA competition," NBA executive vice president and head of basketball operations James Jones said in a statement issued by the league . "We're going to take a really hard stance on flopping. It's something that we'll look at more so than anything." NBA senior vice president and head of referee development and training Monty McCutchen clarified that the exaggerated effort to get a call is what will earn fines from the league, not necessarily the attempt to draw a whistle. "A flop is not merely trying to entice a call. It has to be secondary, theatrical and exaggerated movement," he said. “A lot of these embellishments won't have that STEM — secondary, theatrical, exaggerated movement — and thus would be legal." "Creating a perception of something that you know not to be true, that is separate and needs to be penalized," he added. Under the new initiative, if a player is called for flopping in a game, he will receive a non-unsportsmanlike technical foul and the opposing team gets a free throw. But if the flop is not called during the game, as in George's case, the league can issue a decision after reviewing the play. Players who continue to get punished for flopping will draw an increased amount for a fine and could be issued a one-game suspension after six or more flopping penalties. George was last fined for flopping during the 2023-24 season while with the Los Angeles Clippers, according to Spotrac . During his previous 16 NBA seasons, he's been fined a total of $300,000. That does not include $11.7 million he was docked for being suspended for 25 games without pay last season for violating the league's anti-drug program.

stories.title: Knicks fans name first-born son Knickson Fyve in honor of team's NBA title run
stories.summary: The couple had names picked out before the Knicks beat the Spurs in the NBA Finals.
stories.detailText: Yvonne Gonzalez-Bradford and her husband Vance already had names picked out as the couple approached the final month's of Yvonne's pregnancy with their first child. Lady Victoria if the baby was a girl or Prestige Wisdom if it was a boy. The decision seemed set, but then the New York Knicks beat the San Antonio Spurs in five games in June to win the franchise's first NBA title in 53 years. The historic victory, coupled with the Bradfords finding out they were having a boy, altered their original choice for a name. Yvonne came up with an alternate pick of Knickson, incorporating the name of the Long Island City family's favorite basketball team. A few days later, an idea came up for a middle name: Fyve — as in "Knicks in five." "You know how when something happens so well in your favor, you don't want to jinx it?" Vance told TODAY.com . "I was just like, 'Yep! Absolutely. That's it!'" View this post on Instagram It was 56 days after the Knicks' championship win that Knickson Fyve Bradford was born on Aug. 8. He weighed 8 pounds, 8 ounces and happened to enter the world on Yvonne's birthday. The number eight also has a significant Knicks tie as it is the number of OG Anunoby, whose last-second tip-in basket helped the team complete a 29-point comeback in Game 4 of the NBA Finals. Another Knicks connection to the Bradford family: Vance's mother was the scorekeeper for the 1972-73 team, which went on to win its second NBA title in four seasons. "We wanted to have a very strong and firm name that would lead to a cool life," Vance said. "Knickson Fyve is definitely our motto. Knickson Fyve forever!"

stories.title: LaMelo Ball obviously traveled on way to 3-pointer, NBA refs confirm
stories.summary: The association that represents NBA referees confirmed that LaMelo Ball took two steps too many and traveled in a widely seen clip from Wednesday night's win over Miami.
stories.detailText: MIAMI -- Upon review, Minnesota's LaMelo Ball traveled. Really, really traveled. The association that represents NBA referees posted a clip from Wednesday night's game between the Timberwolves and the Miami Heat and clarified -- not that it needed much clarification -- that Ball indeed did commit a violation on his way to a 3-pointer in the second quarter of Minnesota's win. "For everyone asking, 'how is this legal?' It's not!" the referees' union wrote in a post on X. "He gathers with his right foot on the floor and would be permitted two steps by rule (left-right). He takes four steps after gathering the ball and travels." Even Ball's brother, seven-year NBA player Lonzo Ball, got the call right moments after the play. "Travel lmaoooo," Lonzo Ball posted. Told in an interview with ESPN after the game that his brother made the traveling call, LaMelo Ball -- who was making his Minnesota debut -- still insisted he didn't commit a violation. "He hatin'. He hatin'," LaMelo Ball said in the televised interview. "See, I gotta give him a call right now, cause with the family, he knows what you're supposed to do. Even if I'm wrong, I'm right. That's how it goes." Ball's shouldn't-have-counted shot broke what was a 39-39 tie at the time, but in the end it wasn't like the 3-pointer played a big role in the outcome. LaMelo Ball finished the game with 21 points, and Minnesota won 131-106 .

stories.title: Devin Booker attempts zero threes in Suns’ season-opening 41-point loss
stories.summary: Booker's first game wearing No. 15 ended in a blowout and renewed scrutiny of his perimeter shooting.
stories.detailText: PORTLAND, OREGON - OCTOBER 21: Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns reacts during the second half against the Portland Trail Blazers at Moda Center on October 21, 2026 in Portland, Oregon. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The official debut of Devin Booker wearing number 15 is a game I’m sure he’d rather forget. His team lost by 41 points in the season opener against the Portland Trail Blazers, trailing by as many as 52. Hopefully I forget it too. You can understand why Portland came out and blitzed the Suns. It was an emotional night for the fan base, one they’d been waiting more than a season to experience. After being bought out by Milwaukee in Bradley Beal fashion (the ‘ole 5-year waive and streeeeeetch), Damian Lillard returned to the Trail Blazers in the summer of 2025. But an Achilles injury kept him sidelined for the entirety of last season, leaving all that pent-up excitement surrounding the return of one of the franchise’s most beloved players waiting to be unleashed. And unleashed it was. The Moda Center was in a frenzy. Add newly acquired Ja Morant making his Portland debut, and the recipe was ripe for an emotional tidal wave that the Suns would have to overcome. Overcome it, they did not. “Incredibly emotional to start the game before the jump ball was even tipped,” head coach Jordan Ott said after the game. “They did the better job of using that to their advantage.” Phoenix managed only 12 points in the opening quarter and posted its lowest point total in a season opener since 2017. Coincidentally, that team also lost to the Portland Trail Blazers, surrendering 124 points while scoring only 76. In that game, a third-year Devin Booker managed 12 points on 6-of-17 shooting, including 0-of-3 from beyond the arc. And I know it probably doesn’t mean much in the grand scheme of things, but at least in that game, Booker attempted three-pointers. In this game? Not one. Zip. Zero. Not a single three-point attempt. Does anybody else find that strange? Odd? Your team is getting its teeth kicked in, desperate for points, and…nothing? You’re supposed to be the tip of the offensive spear. You’re the $57 million man. And in a game where your team needs the hemorrhaging to be stopped, you don’t attempt a single shot from beyond the arc? It was only the 17th time in Booker’s 738 career games that he failed to attempt a three-pointer, and the first time he’d done so since November 15, 2024. And wouldn’t you know it? That was another loss in which the Suns scored only 83 points. Fun Fact: That was the night that, following an abysmal performance and the fact that I watched it whilst waiting for the Mariah Carey Christmas Special to start, we introduced Mariah Carey as a Bright Side Baller option. Perhaps the opportunities never presented themselves. Perhaps the smothering defense of former Suns draft pick Toumani Camara (palm, meet face) was too overwhelming for Booker to get a shot off. Perhaps he’s become trigger-shy after posting the second-worst three-point shooting percentage of his career last season (33.0%), compounded by the fact that he went 2-of-16 from deep during the preseason (12.5%). But when you juxtapose that against what we saw from Damian Lillard, who went 6-of-10 from beyond the arc on his way to 25 points, it only added to the embarrassment and frustration of the night. I’m not asking Devin Booker to become Damian Lillard. I’m asking him to recognize what the team needs from him, especially when everything around him is falling apart. We know Booker is an elite midrange scorer. We know he’s never been a high-volume three-point shooter. But at what point does that become a limitation rather than an explanation? The NBA has evolved, and the best offensive players have evolved with it. Booker is entering his 12th season, and we’re still discussing his reluctance to consistently threaten defenses from beyond the arc. “You can always do everything better in a loss like that,” Booker told Duane Rankin of AZ Central in the locker room post-massacre. “Trying to find the flow. We have some work to do and we have some things to learn from.” There’s a significant difference between going 0-of-8 and never attempting one. One represents a willingness to take shots the offense needs, even if they aren’t falling. The other raises questions about why those shots aren’t being taken in the first place. I’m not advocating for contested 30-footers. I’m asking why a player of his caliber can’t generate or recognize opportunities from three over the course of 29 minutes. My concern extends beyond a single game or a single statistical category. It’s about whether the version of Devin Booker we’re watching today is capable of being the offensive engine this team needs him to be. And after last night, I think that’s a perfectly reasonable question to ask. Ultimately, this may have been the result of a bad matchup against a big, long, physical Portland team fueled by the emotional return of one of the franchise’s greatest and most beloved players. But it also brings to the surface some familiar concerns about who Devin Booker is and what he can provide from beyond the arc at this stage of his career. Perhaps these are merely the ramblings and musings of a frustrated fanalyst who went to open his Christmas present, only to discover that instead of the gift he’d been hoping for, he received the proverbial lump of coal. All that excitement, all that anticipation surrounding the start of a new season, and it was immediately ripped away from the fan base. Will Devin Booker have great scoring nights this season? Absolutely. Was this a one-game aberration? We certainly hope so. Maybe Wednesday was an aberration. But if the Suns are going to have any chance of making this season meaningful, they need Booker to be more than an elite midrange scorer. They need him to be a complete offensive threat, and that starts with being willing to take the shots the modern NBA demands. Devin Booker’s debut wearing No. 15 was one to forget. A 41-point loss. Down by as many as 52. And in a game desperate for offense, the $57 million man didn’t attempt a single three-pointer, just the 17th time in 738 career games he hasn't. #D15APPOINTING pic.twitter.com/KtJvtCvtYK — John Voita, III (@DarthVoita) October 22, 2026

stories.title: Walker Kessler had a historic debut against the Warriors
stories.summary: The Lakers big man began 2026-27 with a dominant performance
stories.detailText: LOS ANGELES, CA - OCTOBER 21: Walker Kessler #14 of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on during the game against the Golden State Warriors on October 21, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Pantozzi/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Making his Los Angeles Lakers debut Wednesday night, Walker Kessler put on absolute show inside Crypto.com Arena for his new team and fanbase with 26 points on 12-of-12 shooting, nine rebounds, two blocks and one assist in 30 minutes. His sparkling effort helped Los Angeles rout the Golden State Warriors, 127-105 , to kick off their season with a win. Kessler’s perfect shooting night placed him alongside a couple of historic Lakers big men. His 12-of-12 outing was the second-best shooting performance in franchise history behind a 14-of-14 game from Wilt Chamberlain… Walker Kessler checks out 12/12 from the field, the second-best shooting game in Lakers history behind a 14/14 performance from Wilt Chamberlain. — Dan Woike (@DanWoikeSports) October 22, 2026 …while his staggering 10 dunks joined the company of Shaquille O’Neal: Walker Kessler's 10 dunks are the most by a Laker since Shaq in 2003, per ESPN. — Khobi Price (@khobi_price) October 22, 2026 Despite the excellent debut, Kessler admitted to some pre-game jitters but thoroughly enjoyed his first regular-season appearance in a Lakers uniform and was glad to emerge victorious. ““Yeah, I would say it [lived up to expectations]. It was awesome,” he told reporters postgame. “Got the win, which was the most important thing. I definitely was a little nervous going to the game, but just so thankful and so grateful for how it went.” Among Kessler’s 12 made field goals, five came courtesy of Luka Dončić, who’s been involved in the NBA’s last two double-digit dunk games, a testament to his wondrous playmaking aptitude. 10 dunks made in a game since 2022-23 season: Walker Kessler, LAL vs GSW 10/21/2026 Daniel Gafford, DAL vs UTA 03/21/2024 https://t.co/jis3gEpBmz pic.twitter.com/pFxsAoHrJw — Iztok Franko (@iztok_franko) October 22, 2026 With Dončić and Kessler on the floor together, the Lakers scored 56 points in 18 minutes, good for a hilariously stellar 151.4 offensive rating (small-sample theater is fun!), according to NBA.com. “Very impressive game for him. I think he was 12-12, which is very impressive,” Dončić said. “But just the way he saw, when I was driving, he stepped up. When I was doubled, he played in the pocket. So a very impressive game for him.” Head coach JJ Redick has previously talked about the expectations any notable Lakers big man may experience, especially ahead of their franchise debut. He’s made clear the support system around Kessler to guide him through any worries and was pleased with his center’s first performance of 2026-27. “Whether he had played for the last year and a half or not, I think it’s a big deal when it’s your first game as a Laker,” Redick said. “We’ve had conversations. He understands what this is and the pressures that come with it. I think it was a good opening statement for him.” You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: With The Truth in the building, Celtics give honest perspective on loss to Pistons
stories.summary: There's nothing like having a champ in the building to give you a little perspective.
stories.detailText: (060408 Boston, MA )Boston Celtics forward Paul Pierce and Sam Cassell laughed as the Boston Celtics prepared for game 1 of the NBA Finals at a practice at TD Banknorth Garden on Wednesday, June 4, 2008. Staff Photo by Matthew West. (Photo by Matthew West/MediaNews Group/Boston Herald via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images Yeah, that was a stinker . Despite Paul George turning back the clock for 38 points , the Celtics were out-rebounded and lost the margin battle in the trenches, Jayson Tatum looked off , and Jaylen Brown looked great in a Sixers win over the Knicks on their Ring Night. After building a 22-point lead in their season opener in Detroit, the Celtics were outscored 72-41 in the final 20 minutes that included a Pistons’ 23-0 run. But as bad as Tuesday’s loss was, it’s just the start. “There are bigger adversities in life than losing a game. I’m excited for the challenges and the opportunity,” Joe Mazzulla said at practice on Thursday. “It was a challenge losing that [game], but it’s how you respond to that. It may or may not happen again, but it’s who you become. You have to learn. As I told the team, I don’t want us to feel a certain type of way after a win or after a loss — it’s all the same. You have to be able to process possessions in a game, so it’s really more about the consistency of the approach, not the feeling of the result. We just have to maintain the consistency of the approach and the process and continue to go through that.” With a chance to knock off the defending champion Knicks tomorrow night in their home opener, it’s a quick turnaround for a team looking to turn the page quickly. After a 4-0 successful preseason that seemed to legitimize Mazzulla’s approach, the trade for George, the free agent signings of Mitchell Robinson and Mike Conley Jr., and the development of the Celtics’ growing young core, the team will now have a four-game homestand to settle into the regular season and they don’t seem bothered by the hiccup. “I don’t think it’s concerning. It’s the first game of 82,” Sam Hauser said . “There’s definitely going to be kinks that we have to work out. Obviously we ran into a few things in the last game, but I don’t think we’re concerned. We showed flashes of being really really good and showed flashes of where we need to improve. That’s the battle you go through each and every season.” During training camp, Mazzulla stressed that it’s going to take 10-20 games to see what the team can lean on in terms of their strengths, what needs to be improved, and what the trend lines of the league are going to be. The Pistons, the East’s #1 seed last season, provided a good early test that Mazzulla liked “38 of 48 minutes” of. The key — as it is every year around this time — is being able to do for all 48, night in, night out. “Last game was a perfect game because it was the epitome of momentum and opportunities and turning points and ebbs and flows,” Mazzulla said. He noted that the team generated good shots during their worst stretches against the Pistons, but poor transition defense, fouling three-point shooters, and giving up and-1s off offensive rebounds ultimately allowed Detroit to steamroll them down the stretch. It’s all a learning process in the road to consistency. Mazzulla on Pierce's presence around the Celtics: "The door is open for any Celtic." "It's great to have him around." @CLNSMedia https://t.co/2QZv0mHnx0 pic.twitter.com/lToi7B4RBC — Celtics on CLNS (@CelticsCLNS) October 22, 2026 “The way we want to play, the freedom, the ability to just read the game — it just takes time understanding what each guy likes. We had some really good moments of that, and throughout that process, there will be some janky moments, but we just continue to grow through it, We’re further along than I anticipated from that standpoint,” Mazzulla reiterated. And how’s this for consistency: 26,864 points over 15 regular seasons and a decade’s worth of playoffs. That’s second all-time for the franchise. That’s The Truth. That’s Paul Pierce. The Finals MVP and second all-time leading scorer visited today’s practice at the Auerbach Center. “It makes you want to carry on the Celtics tradition, the legacy when you’ve got them around,” Hauser said of having The Captain back in the building.

stories.title: How Sam Presti's 'slow and steady' trust in SGA created a two-time MVP
stories.summary: The Thunder GM and the two-time MVP have created a partnership that fueled OKC's rise.
stories.detailText: ONE DAY IN the early stages of their relationship, Thunder general manager Sam Presti asked Shai Gilgeous-Alexander to stop by his office to pick up a book. "I was expecting some long book, like full of pages and stories and a bunch of chapters and wisdom and stuff like that," Gilgeous-Alexander told ESPN on the eve of his season-opening win over the San Antonio Spurs . "Have you ever read 'The Tortoise and the Hare'?" Presti asked Gilgeous-Alexander, who was a bit confused by the question. Surely, Presti couldn't have been referring to the classic childhood fable originally composed by the ancient Greek storyteller Aesop. Gilgeous-Alexander figured there must have been "a real book for, like, grown-ups" with the same title. No, Gilgeous-Alexander told Presti, he hadn't read that book. Then Presti pulled out a children's book. "Wait, what? Of course I have," Gilgeous-Alexander said. Presti proceeded to explain how the moral of the book's story applied to Gilgeous-Alexander's development and the GM's vision for the Thunder's evolution into a contender. The gift was a plea for patience from Presti and a promise to travel a slow, steady path to NBA prosperity together. "My journey resonates a lot with that," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "It just kind of made sense." It was a message that particularly applied after Gilgeous-Alexander's second season in Oklahoma City, which was the frustrating first year of Presti's full-blown rebuilding plan. Gilgeous-Alexander had spent much of that season as a spectator, sitting out the second half of the season because of a lingering case of plantar fasciitis while the Thunder took a cautious approach to his treatment and limped to a 22-50 record and lottery pick. His status as the new face of the franchise in Oklahoma City meant he was toiling in national obscurity. Meanwhile, a pair of guards selected before him in the 2018 draft class were thriving on playoff teams. Dallas' Luka Doncic was already a two-time first-team All-NBA selection, and Trae Young had been an All-Star and just led the Atlanta Hawks to an Eastern Conference finals appearance. Memphis' Ja Morant , who was taken in the next draft, had just made his playoff debut and also was widely viewed as an ascending superstar. Gilgeous-Alexander quietly viewed himself as a peer of those other young guards, believing he had just as much potential, a minority opinion at the time but one that Presti shared. Presti reiterated that the Thunder couldn't take shortcuts on the journey to becoming a sustainable contender. As Presti told Gilgeous-Alexander when he gifted him the children's book, "Slow and steady wins the race." During the 2021 offseason, Gilgeous-Alexander and Presti agreed to a five-year, $172 million maximum extension of his rookie contract. Unlike the extensions signed by Doncic and Young that summer, Gilgeous-Alexander's deal did not include a player option, an indication of his allegiance to an OKC franchise that had acquired him along with a historic haul of first-round picks in the Paul George trade with the LA Clippers a couple of years earlier. The contract symbolized the mutual commitment between Gilgeous-Alexander and Presti, a player determined to prove himself and an executive resolute in executing a long-term plan. Five years later, Gilgeous-Alexander is the reigning back-to-back MVP and a 2024-25 championship banner hangs in the Paycom Center rafters. In that hindsight, Gilgeous-Alexander's rookie extension ranks as a remarkable bargain entering the contract's final season before a four-year, $279 million supermax extension begins. At the time, that contract was a calculated gamble that a player who had not yet been an All-Star would blossom. "I just believed wholeheartedly and had trust in just like the human being Sam was," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "In this business, that's another thing that you just can't control -- who runs your organization. I've been lucky to be placed with a guy like Sam. It's been amazing. "It feels like a partnership. I don't work for him. He doesn't work for me. We're in this thing together." GILGEOUS-ALEXANDER SAYS he still feels the sting of being cut from his junior varsity team as a high school freshman in his hometown of Hamilton, Ontario. But he doesn't blame his coach. "There were so many people, like so many people that were in ninth grade at that time that were better than me in basketball," Gilgeous-Alexander said. At the time, he was a skinny kid who had yet to hit his growth spurt and didn't get much playing time on his AAU team. A year later, he earned a starting role on both the varsity squad and his AAU team. He received his first Division I scholarship offer the following summer -- "Binghamton -- never forget it," Gilgeous-Alexander said of what felt like a breakthrough moment. As a senior, Gilgeous-Alexander chose Kentucky over several other offers from high-major programs and was part of Canada's national team program. "I've just been able to outlast and keep getting better, and it's allowed me to get here today," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "And then that formula, I've just kind of just tried to emulate. When I'm not where I want to be or guys that are the same age or around the same class or whatever it is or doing things that I want to do, I just always try to remember that. "It's a long race, just stay down." Gilgeous-Alexander didn't start his career at Kentucky at the front of the pack, either. He was the sixth highest-ranked recruit in the Wildcats' freshman class, behind five top-25 players. He opened the season as a reserve, backing up fellow freshman Quade Green. "There was a list of guys to go see, and he wasn't in the top half of that list coming into the season," Presti said, recalling trips to scout a Kentucky team that eventually sent seven players to the NBA. "But it was funny because you go to see him so many times and he was always the most consistent player. ... I thought that was pretty loud." He ended his lone season at Kentucky as the SEC tournament MVP and a lottery prospect, landing at the No. 11 pick, a few slots behind teammate Kevin Knox II . The Thunder didn't have a first-round pick in 2018, having traded it to the Utah Jazz three years earlier, but Presti still spent plenty of time that season evaluating potential picks. Those evaluations were part of the calculus when Presti brought Gilgeous-Alexander to OKC along with veteran forward Danilo Gallinari and a bundle of draft picks as part of the blockbuster trade that sent George to LA. The Clippers needed to acquire George to seal a free agency commitment from Kawhi Leonard , positioning Presti to cash in on the value of a reigning Finals MVP without ever having his rights. The deal eventually backfired on the Clippers and built the foundation of the Thunder's championship roster. And though the headline of the return was the unprecedented package of draft capital -- five first-rounders and a pair of swaps -- Gilgeous-Alexander represented promise coming off a second-team All-Rookie campaign in which he averaged 10.8 points. "No one could have anticipated what has transpired," Presti said recently, referring to Gilgeous-Alexander's historically elite production as the Thunder morphed into a perennial contender. "So I don't want to make it sound like we knew any of that." ON GILGEOUS-ALEXANDER'S FIRST night in Oklahoma City, Presti poked his head out of his office at the Thunder's practice facility. He had been holed up for hours, negotiating the final touches of the trade that would send Oklahoma City legend Russell Westbrook to the Houston Rockets and working on an op-ed he was writing for The Oklahoman detailing the franchise's decisions and future plans. It was an emotionally exhausting night for Presti, but the sounds of a basketball bouncing and sneakers squeaking provided a bolt of energy. He peaked out onto the court and saw Gilgeous-Alexander going through a workout with members of his inner circle. Presti took comfort in catching that glimpse of Gilgeous-Alexander's serious approach, thinking it might be symbolic that the franchise had already found a worthy successor to Westbrook. It gave him hope that his new point guard could grow into a franchise cornerstone, a gut feeling that has since been reinforced time and again by Gilgeous-Alexander's relentless work ethic. "I have a lot of respect for him as a person," Presti said. "Obviously as a player, it's one thing, but I really respect the way he goes about his craft. When you see somebody that dedicated to the process itself, it makes you want to really advocate for them. It makes you want to help him achieve the things that you know he's capable of achieving. That's built over time." There was just one problem with that scene in late July 2019: Gilgeous-Alexander wasn't wearing official Thunder gear. It had yet to be issued to him, since he hadn't yet held his introductory news conference. It's the sort of seemingly trivial matter that matters a lot to Presti. He still winces when recalling it. Gilgeous-Alexander saw Presti's meticulous attention to detail soon after he stepped onto the court that night. He noticed that every basketball on the ball rack was perfectly placed, connecting the "Spalding" logos in long, continuous lines. It impressed Gilgeous-Alexander that the organization put so much care into such a tiny detail, planting a seed in his mind that Oklahoma City was a place that he could chase his potential. "The greatest of greats obsess over the little things like everyone else does the big things, and it allows them to create a gap," Gilgeous-Alexander said. "The little things over time just keep stacking up, stacking up. All together, the little things become big things." That growth mindset is an essential element of Gilgeous-Alexander's character, which Presti valued as much as his talent. Presti wanted to invest in Gilgeous-Alexander in large part because of "gifts that amplify or make his athletic abilities that much more transcendent," citing intelligence and emotional awareness of others in the organization and community. "Shai puts the wind at everybody's back with the way he operates," Thunder coach Mark Daigneault said. "There's literally no facet, no corner of the building that he doesn't put in a position of strength because of the way that he operates as a superstar player. He can act however he wants to act, as we've seen in the NBA and other sports, and he chooses to act with unbelievable humility and character. It puts everybody in a position of strength, including Sam. With Sam, obviously that's a two-way relationship." THE TORTOISE FOUND a turbo button during the 2022-23 season, the first year of Gilgeous-Alexander's second contract. His scoring soared to 31.4 points per game, an increase of almost seven points from the previous season while improving his efficiency, and he earned his first All-Star bid and All-NBA selection. The Thunder's record improved by 16 games to 40-42, even though No. 2 pick Chet Holmgren sat out the season because of a broken foot . Jalen Williams , selected with a lottery pick acquired from the Clippers, was the Rookie of the Year runner-up. Oklahoma City's foundation was set. With Holmgren healthy, the Thunder made another double-digit win jump the next season, finishing 57-25 to become the youngest No. 1 seed in NBA history. Presti remained patient, opting not to use any of his arsenal of first-round picks to make a splashy trade to expedite the process of constructing a championship team. Gilgeous-Alexander finished second in MVP voting to Nikola Jokic . After a second-round playoff exit to Doncic and the Mavericks in the 2024 playoffs, Presti pounced to acquire a pair of veteran role players as finishing pieces, trading Josh Giddey for title-proven defensive menace Alex Caruso and signing center Isaiah Hartenstein in free agency . The Thunder took another double-digit leap in the win column the next season, going 68-14 as Gilgeous-Alexander claimed the scoring title and his first MVP award before leading Oklahoma City on a championship run. Gilgeous-Alexander hadn't only caught his peers who seemed to have such a big head start only four years earlier. He had put himself into legendary company, joining Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Michael Jordan and Shaquille O'Neal as the only players to win a scoring title, MVP and Finals MVP in the same season . A statue of a tortoise sits alongside those trophies in Gilgeous-Alexander's Oklahoma City home. That was a gift from Presti, a token of gratitude for going on the journey together. "I honestly just believe things had to work out," Gilgeous-Alexander said, adamant that his mind never wandered even while other franchises wondered if he might eventually ask to be traded as losses were piling up in Oklahoma City. "Everybody was just doing the right things to succeed. There was no other universe in my brain. ... But this fast is crazy." Gilgeous-Alexander repeated as MVP last season , becoming only the 14th player to win the award in back-to-back seasons, as Oklahoma City again had the league's best record. The Thunder, weakened by injuries that sidelined Williams and emerging young guard Ajay Mitchell , were eliminated by the Spurs in a Western Conference finals that felt like the first chapter of the league's next epic rivalry. That was a sour start to what the Thunder knew would be a difficult summer for Presti and the front office, simply because of the team's soaring payroll with rookie maximum extensions for Williams and Holmgren kicking in this season. "I will give zero input," Gilgeous-Alexander said after the Thunder's Game 7 loss to the Spurs when asked about personnel decisions on the horizon with Oklahoma City faced with a $213 million luxury tax bill if the roster stayed intact. That was a bit of a white lie. Gilgeous-Alexander respectfully and privately offered his opinion to Presti, particularly lobbying for the Thunder to keep defensive stopper Luguentz Dort , his Canadian countryman and the only other player who remained from his first season in Oklahoma City. But Gilgeous-Alexander understood when Presti made cost-cutting trades to part with a trio of beloved title-winning teammates (Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins ), slashing the Thunder's tax bill to $14 million, as Presti eyes managing the payroll while sustaining a contender through his 28-year-old superstar's prime. His input this summer was more than zero, but Gilgeous-Alexander meant the next line out of his mouth in the wake of the Thunder's exit last season: "I will let Sam Presti, the greatest GM ever, do his job." It's a two-way trust that has been earned and rewarded.

stories.summary: It was only one game, but the Sixers looked like a very cohesive bunch in the opener.

Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images Whenever there are star-laden rosters rolled out in the NBA, skeptics of said rosters often have the same critiques. “There’s only one ball.” “Too many egos.” “Good luck getting that guy to take a back seat to anyone.” The NBA has long been powered by its stars and while it seems as if the narrative in recent years has changed, particularly with a team like New York winning an NBA championship last season primarily due to its stellar depth, top-end talent will always garner a lot of conversation in the NBA. The Sixers have a ton of it. It was fair to question how quickly all of the talent would mesh and come together, but if the season opener at Madison Square Garden was an indication, chemistry isn’t going to be a problem for this season’s Philadelphia 76ers. Every Sixer in the starting lineup, besides VJ Edgecombe who attempted the fewest number of field goals amongst the five, had at least five assists in the 106-100 victory over New York. The Sixers committed fewer turnovers than a Knicks team that was returning the bulk of its roster that won last season’s title. Philadelphia also had 24 fastbreak points to 16 for the Knicks. These are all statistical categories that indicate a strong degree of togetherness and selflessness on the court. On Tuesday night, the Sixers did not look like a team that was still trying to figure out how to put the puzzle pieces together. They also did not beat the Knicks due to a hot shooting night that could just be chalked up to randomness. Philly shot just 28% from the three-point line in the win. They did so with two high-profile new starters in the lineup in LeBron James and Jaylen Brown. They closed out a close game on the road against an opponent that’s owned them in recent seasons including two of the last three postseasons. So if they can do all of that in their first game together against the reigning champions, maybe it’s easy to see why there was so much hype around this team. Inevitably, there are going to be overtures, if they haven’t started already, from fans about coach Nick Nurse’s overreliance on the starting five. Every starter played at least 33 minutes in the opener. There are another 81 regular season games to go plus what the franchise hopes is a deep playoff run. Managing minutes is not a novel concept for Nurse, but how good will he be at it this season? It’s a fair question. Will Mike Gansey be able to find a backup center to Joel Embiid after losing Ariel Hukporti for the year before the season started? Finding some consistent outside shooting from the wing also figures to be the easiest way to get James some rest throughout the marathon that is the regular season. Surely, there are still things the Sixers will have to figure out during the season as they’re not going to waltz to an NBA championship. But playing into June was on everyone’s minds before this season started and the victory on Tuesday night in New York showed us why. Chemistry and cohesion are usually things that only get better as the season goes on and if that’s the case for this group, we might be in for a very special next 6-8 months, Sixers fans.

stories.title: LaMelo Ball got away with the most blatant travel you will ever see
stories.summary: Right in front of the official. The NBA really is back.
stories.detailText: There is uncalled traveling in the NBA, and then there is what LaMelo Ball did on Wednesday night. "That's a travel." How many steps from LaMelo? pic.twitter.com/pmuhYg1zQb — SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) October 22, 2026 That's not a travel, that's a vacation. It was right in front of the official — who should have been focused on Ball's feet, making sure he was behind the arc. To the credit of the official NBA referees account, they owned that this was a missed call. For everyone asking, “how is this legal?” It’s not! He gathers with his right foot on the floor and would be permitted two steps by rule (left-right). He takes four steps after gathering the ball and travels. https://t.co/dSitGeRNSD — NBA Referees (@OfficialNBARefs) October 22, 2026 Don't let this take away from Ball's impressive Timberwolves debut: 21 points and six assists in 28 minutes, and he was +18. It also helped that Anthony Edwards was on a heater. But that absolutely was a travel.

stories.title: Mavericks coach Dusty May breaks down Flagg’s, Irving’s season-opening performances against Rockets
stories.summary: The 2026-27 season didn’t start off the way the Dallas Mavericks had hoped.
stories.detailText: HOUSTON, TEXAS - OCTOBER 21: Kyrie Irving #11 of the Dallas Mavericks speaks with Cooper Flagg #32 during the second quarter of the game against the Houston Rockets at Toyota Center on October 21, 2026 in Houston, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Dallas Mavericks’ 2026-27 season got off to a rocky start on Wednesday night, as they got blown out by Kevin Durant and the Houston Rockets, 128-110. After only trailing 32-26 when the first quarter ended, the Mavs proceeded to get outscored 38-12 in the second quarter, which ended up being the deciding factor in the game. Dallas outscored Houston 72-58 in the second half, but it was already too late. It was a little bit of a mixed bag when it came to the performances of the Mavs’ two stars, 19-year-old Cooper Flagg and 34-year-old Kyrie Irving, who was playing his first real NBA game in nearly 600 days following an ACL injury. Flagg finished with a game-high 32 points (10-17 FG, 11-13 FT), five rebounds, two assists, three steals and one block in 33 minutes of action. He poured in 23 of his 32 points in the second half alone. Irving finished with 15 points (6-9 FG), four rebounds, two assists and one steal. Both Flagg and Irving had four turnovers each. Following the loss, Mavs head coach Dusty May gave his thoughts on how his two stars played in their first real game together. “I thought he was setting us up,” May said of Flagg’s second-half scoring. “In the first half I thought he was being very intentional with getting his teammates shots, and then, in the second half, we did a better job of getting some off-ball movement. We played a little bit faster, and then obviously if you’re not taking the ball out of the net, you can get it up and attack quickly. I thought that was the biggest difference. We just — our pace got a lot better in the second half.” Getting to the free-throw line was something Dallas struggled with in the preseason, so Flagg’s ability to get to the stripe 13 times and convert 11 of them was a welcome sight for May. “That’s been a point of emphasis, and that’s one thing, when we evaluated ourselves after four [preseason] games, getting to the line wasn’t something we did well,” May said. “We thought [Flagg] was the best way to capitalize in the paint. I thought he was strong. I thought he made good decisions. When we start knocking down some open shots, his assist numbers will increase.” Irving was efficient on Wednesday night, but the problem was that his shots were limited. That obviously wasn’t by May’s design, but it’s what the Rockets’ defense forced the Mavs into. “He’s obviously the focal point,” May said of Irving being limited to nine field-goal attempts by Houston’s defense. “They put two on the ball. I thought he made the right plays, the right decisions. There [are] going to be puzzles we’re going to have to figure out. Playing four-on-three with our other guys — we’ve got to do a better job and find some solutions. “But I thought there in the second half, he showed a real — his true character — in being a leader when things weren’t going well, I thought he set a great example. Our bench was phenomenal. They were cheering for each other. We’re worried about getting better, especially starting with a couple games on the road like we are. We’re focused on getting better, and I was proud of the way the guys stayed connected and stayed fighting until the end. That showed some character.” The Mavs now shift their attention to another road test against the Indiana Pacers on Friday night before opening up at home against the San Antonio Spurs on Saturday night. The Pacers started their season off 1-0 with a 123-120 win over the New Orleans Pelicans after star point guard Tyrese Haliburton made his return from an achilles injury he suffered in the 2025 NBA Finals. “[We have to] learn from what we did well,” May said. “I thought we made some strides in areas we’ve struggled in. But just look at the film. The lowest-hanging fruit — what can we fix in a 48-hour period, so we’re not out here chasing every rabbit, but focus on a couple of things so we can just trust it a little bit more. From everybody, we’ll fix that area. … These extra possessions, they steamroll on you, so if we just clean up a few things, I think we’ll make a significant jump.”

stories.title: Donovan Mitchell wants to be in Cleveland ‘forever’
stories.summary: Mitchell doesn’t plan on going anywhere.
stories.detailText: CLEVELAND, OHIO - APRIL 18: Donovan Mitchell #45 of the Cleveland Cavaliers celebrates during the first quarter of Game One of the Eastern Conference First Round NBA Playoffs against the Toronto Raptors at Rocket Arena on April 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Cavaliers took a risk when they traded for Donovan Mitchell in 2022. They made a gamble that the assets they unloaded, which included multiple first-round picks that spanned seven years, would ultimately never be missed. It looks like they’re winning that bet. “I don’t ever want to wear another uniform,” Mitchell said in a Cleveland.com exclusive with Chris Fedor. “I dream of myself being here forever and hopefully having 45 in the rafters one day.” Mitchell has not only led the franchise to some of their most successful seasons, but he’s signed an extension that keeps him in Cleveland through the 2029-30 NBA season — past the date of the final draft pick that is owed to the Utah Jazz. There was a time when it was unclear if the Cavs would retain Mitchell for more than a single season. Or if they’d reach an agreement on even one contract extension. But now we are two extensions deep with a franchise star who has fully committed to the city he’s in. Mitchell has averaged 26.7 points and 5.3 assists in four seasons with the Cavaliers. He’s been an All-Star in each season and was named to an All-NBA team in three of the four. Entering his fifth year in Cleveland, Mitchell has made it clear that this is where he wants to be. The franchise has doubled and tripled down on their own commitment to him. Trading for James Harden last season and shuffling the starting lineup to add a 3-and-D wing in Peyton Watson. It’s all built around competing now while Mitchell’s window is open. The Cavs haven’t had many players of Mitchell’s caliber represent the city, let alone retire in Cleveland. There’s something to be said for a star embracing his new home — even if this is all easier said than done. A lot can change between now and the end of Mitchell’s career, but a verbal commitment like this shouldn’t be taken for granted.

stories.title: Inside Caleb Williams' group of famous Chicago sports friends
stories.summary: Bears QB Caleb Williams is part of a trio of young Chicago athletes whose friendship transcends sports.
stories.detailText: Matas Buzelis started his postgame treatment the night of Jan. 10 shortly after the Chicago Bulls beat the Dallas Mavericks . Less than five miles away from the training room inside the United Center, the blustery conditions on the lakefront were the backdrop for the Chicago Bears ' fourth-quarter fight in a wild-card playoff thriller. Buzelis had a special interest in the game. As the then-21-year-old small forward lowered himself into a cold tub filled with ice water, Buzelis watched his friend Caleb Williams go to work. Buzelis, the Bulls' 2024 first-round pick, doesn't claim to be much of a football fan, but he understood the significance of what he was witnessing as a Chicago native. Williams, one of Buzelis' closest confidants, was in the midst of a career-defining moment when he led the Bears back from a 21-3 halftime deficit to beat the Green Bay Packers 31-27. Buzelis recalls celebrating "that crazy throw" Williams made on fourth-and-8 to Rome Odunze that kept a touchdown drive alive. Inside a suite at Soldier Field, Chicago Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong erupted as Odunze made the catch. "My head was about touching the ceiling," Crow-Armstrong told ESPN. "We were all jumping up and down. I feel like that's something you can't really [describe]. Maybe a walk-off homer or something like that evokes sort of a similar feeling, but that one's tough to beat." That game helped elevate Williams from an ascending, young quarterback into national stardom. The play -- specifically Williams' jump pass -- was commemorated on the cover of "Madden NFL 27." Williams' "Ice Man" nickname started generating national buzz, and he emerged as the most recognizable star in Chicago sports. But he has company. And the Williams-PCA-Buzelis group text chat should be popping Thursday after the Bears host the New England Patriots (8:15 p.m., ET, Prime Video). The increased visibility and expectations for the Bears (4-2, 0-2 NFC North) in Williams' third season is what he has been primed to manage his whole career. At every juncture, from winning the Heisman Trophy at USC to becoming the first overall pick in 2024, the quarterback has followed a curated plan to keep grounded. A big part of that includes the people he welcomes into his circle. In Chicago, the place where Williams says he wants to be forever, he does so in close proximity to others who hold an intimate understanding of the type of demands he encounters daily. Because they, too, navigate a similar burden of success. "This isn't even about us going against each other, but that's how we look at it," Buzelis said. "We want to one-up each other every time. "We see Pete hit three home runs in one game. Now we want to do something in our sport that's that outstanding in that type of manner, but it's all about us competing against each other. I'd say Caleb had a great game. Now I'm looking forward to my season, and that's the excitement it brings of all of us knowing each other." What it's like hanging out with Caleb Williams The three-member group chat lights up multiple times a week. It's the way these 20-somethings with hectic, conflicting schedules stay connected, whether to offer words of encouragement, share TikToks and memes or plan an outing. "We just talk a bunch of s--- and also love on each other as well," said Crow-Armstrong, 24, who's expected to be named the National League MVP on Nov. 12. The Cubs slugger made his major league debut in September 2023, more than two years after the New York Mets traded him to Chicago. In the spring of 2024, Williams became the first quarterback selected by the Bears with the top pick in the draft. In June 2024, the Bulls drafted Buzelis 11th. The foundation of Williams and Buzelis' friendship was set during the quarterback's junior season at USC, where the former NBA G Leaguer's team trained. The two snapped a photo after one of Buzelis' practices and stayed in touch as they both made their way to Chicago. Crow-Armstrong and Williams were a more traditional Gen Z match by following each other on social media and trading direct messages back and forth. When plans make it out of the chat, the group expands to include Odunze and Cole Bennett, the Illinois native and Lyrical Lemonade founder who has directed over 500 music videos for the industry's biggest artists, from Eminem to Future. Bennett met Williams the year after his Heisman campaign when the quarterback asked him to direct an eventual documentary on his life and career. "I left the first time we ever met feeling like, oh no, he's a superstar and he knows it," Bennett said. "It's a really unique trait because it's really hard to walk that line of being incredibly confident and not being arrogant but being uniquely yourself and knowing the path that you're on. And he's figured it out." Conversations about shared passions, sports and music are held over s'mores and bonfires at Bennett's Chicago-area home. These are sacred occurrences because of how difficult it can be aligning schedules; evenings that hold special meaning for the space they create for vulnerability away from the spotlight. "We just sit, talk, we get to vent if we need to about anything that's on our minds," Buzelis said. "Everyone's understanding in that group, and they know the caliber of what we're talking about." Other nights it's bowling, showing up at each other's games or attempting to move inconspicuously as they leave restaurants whose reservations are nearly impossible to snag. Lately, it's no surprise who among the group gets recognized the fastest. "When I go out with him, it's always about Caleb, and personally I kind of like that," Crow-Armstrong said. "It's a different kind of night out when he's around just because people f---ing love the dude." Williams had "no room to breathe" when he and Crow-Armstrong sat on the glass for the Chicago Blackhawks - Winnipeg Jets game in January, one day removed from the Bears' season ending in the divisional round of the playoffs. Like Williams, Blackhawks' captain Connor Bedard was also drafted first overall and carries the mantle of a franchise savior. The night before the Bears- Los Angeles Rams divisional playoff game on Jan. 18, Bedard arrived at the United Center for the Blackhawks game against the Bruins wearing Williams' orange Bears jersey. "I wanted to order one, but obviously it wouldn't get there the day of, so I DoorDashed that [the night before the game]," Bedard told reporters. Williams returned the show of support on Jan. 19, donning Bedard's No. 98 sweater as he and Crow-Armstrong were mobbed by fans as they climbed the aisle from their seats. It was a similar scene the following night as Williams and Crow-Armstrong's offseason tour de Chicago sports continued. Buzelis was reminded that his friends were in attendance by the loud ovation Williams and Crow-Armstrong received when shown on the jumbotron. Sitting on the baseline for Bulls- LA Clippers , the two cheered as Buzelis dropped 21 points in the win. "Once I hear them coming, I want to put on a show," said Buzelis, who made All-Rookie second team after the 2024-25 season. "And that's something I've been approaching in every game, not just when they show up, but them showing up shows how real they are and what kind of friendship we have." When Williams went incognito at a Kanye West concert As the Bears broke training camp in early September and were given four days off, Williams hauled it from Halas Hall to Wrigley Field through heavy Chicago traffic to take advantage of the only respite he would get until after the season. His group, which included Buzelis, Bennett and Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson , arrived just in time to watch PCA launch his 39th home run of the season into center field, powering the Cubs to a 2-1 victory over the division rival Milwaukee Brewers . Williams' group had tickets in a private suite but relinquished them in favor of a front-row view. "I like being out with the people supporting one of my friends, Cubbie Pete, and so it was just kind of spur of the moment, wanted to sit out there," Williams said. Crow-Armstrong wasn't aware his friends had witnessed another milestone on his way to becoming the seventh player in MLB history to hit 40 home runs and steal 40 bases. It wasn't until he heard the "P-C-A" chants started by Buzelis, "all seven feet of goofy," Crow-Armstrong laughs. Williams and the rest of the crew clad in PCA's pinstriped jersey joined in and started slapping the top of the home dugout, prompting the center fielder to turn around and smile. "You just get to feed off of that," Crow-Armstrong said. "As much as he is my friend, it juices me up when the quarterback of the Chicago Bears is getting people to chant for me." The spotlight belonged to Crow-Armstrong that evening as the group celebrated his triumph and posed for pictures together in the locker room. The following night, Williams avoided the spotlight completely. On the second night of Kanye West's sold-out homecoming concert at Soldier Field, Williams swapped his celebrity for anonymity. "He had a suite ticket, and I was like, 'I'm going to watch it on the floor,'" Bennett said. "'I want to experience this. I want to be in there.' "He's like, 'I want to do it too.' I was like, 'All right, if you do it, you need to wear a mask and glasses. You have to really, really be incognito.' So, he came and was all masked up with glasses on, and no one recognized him, not a single person." On the same field where he set the Bears' single-season passing record (3,942 yards) and gives tens of thousands of fans that pour into the stadium for games a reason to believe in the direction of the franchise, Williams immersed himself in the crowd wearing a black ski mask and dark sunglasses. For that night, he got to be a normal 24-year-old, simply one of nearly 71,000 fans in attendance, not his usual experience of being the one fans come to watch. These moments and those with whom he has gotten to experience them keeps Williams grounded through a season that will undoubtedly shape the next chapter of his career in the NFL. In a city that he has grown to love surrounded by the relationships that support his ascension, Chicago holds a special place for Williams. "I obviously want to be here forever," Williams said. "That's a goal of mine. "When I made my goals, [it's] to be at one place until I'm done, until I decide that it's over for me and I want to go home and ride off into the sun."

stories.title: Mitchell Robinson had a strong reaction to his Celtics debut
stories.summary: Robinson took ownership for the Celtics opening day loss to the Pistons: “I’m one of the best defensive bigs in this league, and I didn’t show it that night.”
stories.detailText: DETROIT, MI - OCTOBER 20: Mitchell Robinson #4 of the Boston Celtics shoots the ball during the game against the Detroit Pistons on October 20, 2026 at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Chris Schwegler/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images BOSTON — Mitchell Robinson didn’t mince words at Celtics practice Thursday morning, less than 48 hours after his lackluster Celtics debut. In the Celtics’ 121-113 loss to the Detroit Pistons, Robinson tallied 4 points, 2 assists, 2 blocks, and 2 turnovers in 18 minutes. The normally prolific rebounder couldn’t make his impact on the glass, grabbing just 3 boards, only 1 of which came on the offensive end. “It’s obviously just my fault,” Robinson said. “I got to accept that, and obviously be better from here on out. It’s straightforward — my fault.” Robinson pointed to his lack of defensive impact as one of the main issues with his performance. “We didn’t keep our foot on the gas, and it starts with me,” he said. “I’m one of the best defensive bigs in this league, and I didn’t show it that night. I got to take ownership of that; I gotta be better.” The 28-year-old did go down with a twisted ankle in the second quarter of Tuesday’s game, but returned shortly after. On Thursday, he said the ankle injury didn’t factor into his performance. Looks like Mitchell Robinson hurt his ankle – he’s hobbling off the floor in pain pic.twitter.com/gOHLh1XKka — Noa Dalzell 🏀 (@NoaDalzell) October 20, 2026 “You tweak an ankle, you’re going to feel it a little bit here and there, but shit happens,” Robinson said. “I just felt like I was playing like trash the whole time anyways. I mean, shit.” Robinson isn’t worried about putting points on the board. But his interior presence and rebounding got him a 3-year, $47 million contract, and he prioritizes those on any given night. “Once I feel good about that after the game, for me, that’s when I know I did pretty good,” he said. “I really don’t care about stat lines, scoring; we got that over here already. It’s like — what can I do to help my team?” Joe Mazzulla spoke with Robinson after the game Mitchell Robinson said last week that Joe Mazzulla has been hard on him since he arrived in Boston. “He’s getting on my ass a lot,” he said. “Which, you know, I need that. But he gets on my ass.” But after Robinson’s frustrating game, Mazzula reached out in an encouraging fashion. “Joe’s a great guy,” Robinson said. “He talked me through a lot of things, especially that night. He sent me text messages and stuff like that, and I appreciate it, but I didn’t even respond to the last text. But I was still stuck in my head about it. Like, I played like ass.” Mazzulla said he recognizes Robinson’s importance and expects him to keep acclimating over time. “It’s game one, obviously, and again, for us, he’s a very important piece to what we do, and so the standard is a little bit higher, and the expectation is a little bit higher,” Mazzulla said. “So I think it just comes with time, understanding that every play, you’re at the nucleus of what we’re trying to accomplish on both ends of the floor, and it’s a great compliment that all three of those bigs share. And some of that just comes with time — just the offensive reads, the offensive chemistry, the offensive execution, but also the defensive reads and the defensive reactions that we have to have. I appreciate that he’s in that space, and I think he’s taking on the responsibility and knowing how important that position is.” Robinson said last week he’s enjoying his more involved role, even though there’s been an acclimation period. “I’m in a lot of actions on the offensive side,” Robinson said. “Over there, I was just like, set one screen, roll, and they’ll be going on the other side, and then maybe come back. But like, this one, I’m in like every action. I’m setting the flare, pin down, ball screen, whatever. Like I’m just always actively moving.” Mitchell Robinson will face his old Knicks teammates on Friday On Friday, Robinson will face the New York Knicks, the team he spent his first 8 years with. The Knicks also come off an opening-day loss, a 106-100 defeat to the Philadelphia 76ers. But though Robinson is excited to put Tuesday behind him, he said he doesn’t have extra emotion or motivation specifically because of the Knicks match-up. “It doesn’t really matter that I’m playing my former team,” he said. “It’s more so just trying to bounce back from what happened two nights ago. At the end of the day, it’s basketball; it’s a business. And, you got to play the team just like you play any other team.”

stories.title: Kawhi Leonard was itching to play more in Raptors return but has no timeline on reaching midseason form: 'You can't rush greatness'
stories.summary: Leonard asked head coach Darko Rajaković to let him back into the game in the fourth quarter of a season-opening blowout win over the Chicago Bulls.
stories.detailText: After the NBA investigation surrounding the Los Angeles Clippers' salary cap circumvention delayed a trade that ultimately sent Kawhi Leonard back to the Toronto Raptors , the 35-year-old Leonard was left with a limited runway to the regular season. With reduced preseason work, the two-time NBA Finals MVP has found himself antsy for more game reps, so much so that he asked back into a season-opening blowout of the Chicago Bulls on Wednesday night in Toronto. That said, after scoring 23 points on just 5-of-17 shooting in the 135-92 victory , Leonard isn't putting a date on when he'll return to midseason form. "You can't rush greatness," Leonard said postgame, when a reporter inquired if the seven-time All-Star had a target for when he'd like to be at that level again. "Whenever the medical [staff] thinks I could push forward and I'm feeling great, whatever numbers we're looking at or they're looking at, then that's when that time will come. So yeah, I'm just happy to be out there and try to do the best I can with my minutes." Leonard bargained for more Wednesday, finishing with 24. In the process, he also piled up 6 rebounds, 4 steals, 2 assists and 1 block. "I really love the fact there that he asked to play more minutes in the fourth quarter just to get his legs under him," head coach Darko Rajaković said. Rajaković later added: "We had a plan for him, but he was like, 'Coach, I would like to play a little bit more there.' So, I mean, the game was kind of at that point a little bit out of the reach, but I wanted just to save him, and he was like, 'No, no, I want to go back.' So I put him back." The Toronto Raptors' season-opening fan giveaway at Scotiabank Arena in Toronto on Oct. 21 commemorated the return of Kawhi Leonard with a T-shirt that features his hand, which is responsible for Leonard's signature nickname, "The Klaw." Steve Russell via Getty Images The Raptors also got 20-plus points from three other players: RJ Barrett had 20 on the dot, and both Scottie Barnes and Immanuel Quickley clocked out with 23 points. But the attention was on Leonard, who was playing in his first regular-season game for the Raptors since the 2018-19 campaign, which culminated in Toronto's lone NBA championship. On Tuesday, Leonard posted a video essay on social media ahead of that highly anticipated game. In it, he said, "I'm not here to live in the past. I'm here for what's next. Here in the North, we got a young team. Hungry and ready. And just like we had our moment, we trying to shock the world, again." As I Return. pic.twitter.com/yMv1iqMt30 — Kawhi Leonard (@Way2Whi) October 20, 2026 Leonard said after Wednesday's game that the post was for the fans, to show them that he genuinely cares about the season and that he's going to connect with them along the way. "Just a fan interaction and just connection, really," said a noticeably open Leonard. "You'll probably see a little bit more of me, what I'm doing in the community and just personality …" Leonard's personality has been veiled at times throughout his NBA career. Following the Raptors' first regular-season outing, though, he was introspective and willing to share. "Me being the oldest on the team, being 35, I have to give them that pedigree, that experience of the will to win," Leonard said after being asked about how he sees himself in a mentor role. "And even when we're down, just making sure that everybody's enjoying the moment and knowing that in hard times, that's what makes you better, especially on nights when the ball's not going in. I feel like those are the special nights because you have to dig deep and grind it out or just think forward, forward think. Everybody could come and play well when shots are falling. That's the easiest game. So it's always great to have a challenge." Wednesday was one of those challenges for Leonard. He overcame it with 11 free throws and a diverse defensive impact. On a night that featured his "Klaw" on the fan giveaway T-shirts, his fingerprints were fittingly all over the game, regardless of his capped minutes and shooting struggles.

stories.detailText: Los Angeles Lakers’ Walker Kessler tallied 10 dunks during his team’s 127–105 win over the Golden State Warriors Wednesday night. Those 10 dunks were the most a Laker has produced in a game since the days of Shaquille O’Neal back in 2003. Following the win, Kessler’s overall performance against the Warriors — scoring 26 points on perfect 12-for-12 shooting from the field — earned high praise from Shaq himself. Walker Kessler tallied 10 dunks during the Lakers’ 127–105 win over the Golden State Warriors on Wednesday night. NBAE via Getty Images “For so long, the Lakers’ big men have been historical and dominant. Walker Kessler is the best big man in the NBA. You heard it here first,” O’Neal said from the ESPN studio. The NBA on ESPN’s Instagram account posted a clip of Shaq’s comment on Wednesday night, which was then reposted by Kessler’s fiancée, former Miss America winner Abbie Stockard , on Thursday morning. Kessler’s fiancée, former Miss America winner Abbie Stockard, reposted it to her own Instagram story Thursday. Kessler’s 10 dunks were the most a Lakers player has produced in a game since Shaquille O’Neal back in 2003. Beauty queen Stockard recently finished nursing school in Alabama, so it’s unclear whether she’s currently with Kessler in Los Angeles as he embarks on his debut season with the Lakers. Regardless, whatever mutual support Kessler and Stockard have going on at home is translating to success on the basketball court.
